claims.claim: Expression of ApoE is reduced in uninfected Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
claims.source: Interestingly, expression of several non-ISG, non-immune genes was reduced in uninfected Lrrk2 KO BMDMs, including ApoE, which has been repeatedly linked to inflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases, and Ldhb, a critical metabolic gene involved in post-glycolytic energy production (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Expression of Ldhb is reduced in uninfected Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
claims.source: Interestingly, expression of several non-ISG, non-immune genes was reduced in uninfected Lrrk2 KO BMDMs, including ApoE, which has been repeatedly linked to inflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases, and Ldhb, a critical metabolic gene involved in post-glycolytic energy production (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Lrrk2 KO macrophages exhibit a significant defect in ISG expression 8 hr post-infection with Mycobacterium leprae.
claims.source: We measured a significant defect in ISG expression 8 hr post-infection in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs and Lrrk2 KO RAW 264.7 macrophages compared to control cells (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Transfection of immunostimulatory dsDNA (ISD) induces blunted Ifnb expression in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
claims.source: Transfection of immunostimulatory dsDNA (ISD), which is recognized by cGAS and stimulates the STING/TBK1/IRF3 axis, induced blunted Ifnb expression in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs (Figure 2B), Lrrk2 KO peritoneal macrophages (PEM) (significant differences in Ifnb expression were measured between Lrrk2 KO and HET at baseline but induction differences failed to reach statistical significance via 2-way ANOVA Tukey post-hoc testing) (Figure 2C), Lrrk2 KO RAW 264.7 macrophages (Figure 2D), Lrrk2 KO mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) (Figure 2E), and Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 macrophages (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2B-F.

claims.claim: Lrrk2 KO BMDMs fail to fully induce Ifnb when stimulated with DMXAA.
claims.source: We also found that Lrrk2 KO BMDMs failed to fully induce Ifnb if we bypassed cGAS and stimulated the DNA sensing adapter STING directly using the agonist DMXAA (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: Lrrk2 KO macrophages show a significant defect in the ability to signal through IFNAR (phospho-STAT1).
claims.source: In support of a defect in cytosolic nucleic acid sensing and IFNAR signaling, western blot analysis of IRF3 (phospho-Ser396) and STAT1 (phospho-Tyr701) activation showed a significant defect in the ability of Lrrk2 KO macrophages to signal through IFNAR (phospho-STAT1) and a modest defect in cytosolic DNA sensing (phospho-IRF3) over the course of 6 hr following ISD transfection (Figure 2H, quantitation below, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: Lrrk2 KO macrophages show a modest defect in cytosolic DNA sensing (phospho-IRF3).
claims.source: In support of a defect in cytosolic nucleic acid sensing and IFNAR signaling, western blot analysis of IRF3 (phospho-Ser396) and STAT1 (phospho-Tyr701) activation showed a significant defect in the ability of Lrrk2 KO macrophages to signal through IFNAR (phospho-STAT1) and a modest defect in cytosolic DNA sensing (phospho-IRF3) over the course of 6 hr following ISD transfection (Figure 2H, quantitation below, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: Lrrk2 KO BMDMs are defective in ISG expression following recombinant bioactive IFN-β treatment.
claims.source: Lrrk2 KO BMDMs were, however, defective in ISG expression following recombinant bioactive IFN-β treatment (which directly engages with IFNAR) (Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2J.

claims.claim: Treatment with an IFN-β neutralizing antibody reduces basal levels of ISGs in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
claims.source: Indeed, when HET and KO Lrrk2 BMDMs were treated with an IFN-β neutralizing antibody, there was a reduction in basal levels of Isg15 and Irf7 in Lrrk2 KO cells (Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2K.

claims.claim: Loss of IFNAR signaling reduces basal ISG levels in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
claims.source: We next tested if loss of IFNAR signaling could similarly rescue the Lrrk2 KO phenotype by crossing Lrrk2 KO mice to Ifnar KO mice. In Lrrk2/Ifnar double KO BMDMs, we also observed a significant reduction in basal ISG levels (Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2L.

claims.claim: Loss of cGAS significantly reduces basal ISG expression in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
claims.source: Although basal Isg15 expression differences between Lrrk2 KO and HET BMDMs were more modest in this experiment, loss of cGAS significantly reduced basal ISG expression in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: cGas/Lrrk2 double KO macrophages respond normally to DMXAA and poly(I:C) transfection.
claims.source: With lowered resting type I IFN levels, cGas/Lrrk2 double KOs were able to respond normally to IFN/ISG-generating innate immune stimuli like DMXAA, which bypasses cGAS and stimulates STING directly (Diner et al., 2013), and poly(I:C) transfection (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Levels of STAT1 phosphorylation are restored in cGas/Lrrk2 double KO macrophages.
claims.source: Consistent with the ability of cGas ablation to rescue Lrrk2 KO baseline and induction defects, western blot analysis showed that levels of STAT1 phosphorylation were restored in cGas/Lrrk2 double KOs (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Lrrk2 KO MEFs have a more fragmented mitochondrial network, especially around the cell periphery.
claims.source: As previously described for cells overexpressing wild-type or mutant alleles of LRRK2 (Yang et al., 2014), Lrrk2 KO MEFs had a more fragmented mitochondrial network, especially around the cell periphery, as evidenced by punctate TOM20 staining (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 macrophages have ~3 fold more cytosolic mtDNA compared to controls.
claims.source: We found that although Lrrk2 KD cells had only slightly higher total mtDNA compared to controls (Figure 3D), they had ~3 fold more cytosolic mtDNA (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: TFAM and VDAC are not detectable in the cytosolic fraction of Lrrk2 KD cells by western blot.
claims.source: This increase in cytosolic mtDNA was not simply an artifact of fragmented mitochondria contaminating cytosolic fractions as neither TFAM, an abundant mitochondrial transcription factor, nor VDAC, a mitochondrial outer membrane protein, were detectable in the cytosolic fraction by western blot (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Depleting TFAM in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs leads to even higher basal ISG expression.
claims.source: To exacerbate the proposed mitochondrial defect, we crossed Lrrk2 KO mice with Tfam HET mice. Tfam HET mice are deficient in the mitochondrial transcription factor required for maintaining the mtDNA network and thus have high levels of cytosolic mtDNA (Kasashima et al., 2011; West et al., 2015). Depleting TFAM in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs led to even higher basal ISG expression (Figure 3G), further suggesting that release of mtDNA into the cytosol in Lrrk2 KO cells contributes to their elevated type I IFN expression.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Treating Lrrk2 KO RAW 264.7 cells with ddC substantially reduces mtDNA copy number.
claims.source: We next sought to rescue type I IFN defects in Lrrk2 KO macrophages by depleting mtDNA using ddC (2',3'-dideoxycytidine), an inhibitor of mtDNA synthesis (Leibowitz, 1971; Meyer and Simpson, 1969). Treating Lrrk2 KO RAW 264.7 cells with ddC substantially reduced mtDNA copy number (Figure 3H) and resulted in similar basal expression of type I IFN and ISGs in resting Lrrk2 HET and KO cells (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: mtDNA depletion with ddC restores the ability of Lrrk2 KO macrophages to induce Ifnb in response to ISD.
claims.source: Importantly, when mtDNA-depleted Lrrk2 KO RAW 264.7 macrophages were stimulated with ISD, their ability to induce Ifnb was restored to that of wild-type; Lrrk2 KO macrophages induced Ifnb approximately 500-fold in the absence of ddC but approximately 5000-fold following ddC treatment while WT macrophages induced Ifnb between 4000–5000-fold +/- ddC treatment (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3I.

claims.claim: Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 cells have significantly higher levels of phospho-S616 DRP1 compared to controls.
claims.source: Because DRP1 is known to be positively regulated via phosphorylation at Ser616 (Taguchi et al., 2007), we performed flow cytometry with an antibody specific for phospho-S616 DRP1 and observed significantly higher levels of phospho-S616 DRP1 in Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 cells, Lrrk2 KO BMDMs, and Lrrk2 KO MEFs compared to controls (Figure 4A,C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A, C, and D.

claims.claim: DRP1 inhibition with Mdivi-1 returns ISG expression to control levels in Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 macrophages and Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
claims.source: Next, to test if DRP1 activity was linked to high basal type I IFN/ISG expression in Lrrk2 deficient cells, we chemically inhibited DRP1 with Mdivi-1 and measured basal gene expression levels. In Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 macrophages and Lrrk2 KO BMDMs, DRP1 inhibition returned ISG expression to control levels (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: DRP1 inhibition restores cytosolic mtDNA levels to those of control cells in Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 cells and Lrrk2 KO MEFs.
claims.source: DRP1 inhibition also restored the cytosolic mtDNA levels in Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 cells and Lrrk2 KO MEFs to those of control cells (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Lrrk2 KO BMDMs have lower mitochondrial membrane potential compared to control cells.
claims.source: Flow cytometry analysis of resting Lrrk2 HET and KO cells revealed lower levels of JC-1 dye aggregation (i.e., lower mitochondrial membrane potential) in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs (Figure 5A–B), Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 macrophages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and primary Lrrk2 KO MEFs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), compared to control cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using JC-1 dye shown in Figure 5A-B.

claims.claim: Lrrk2 KO BMDMs are more sensitive to mitochondrial damaging agents rotenone/ATP and FCCP.
claims.source: In addition, Lrrk2 KO BMDMs were more sensitive to the mitochondrial damaging and depolarizing agents, rotenone/ATP and FCCP, as measured by both JC-1 (Figure 5C; RAW 264.7 Lrrk2 KDs and Lrrk2 KO MEFs in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B, respectively) and TMRE (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claims.claim: Treatment with Mdivi-1 normalizes mitochondrial membrane potential in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
claims.source: Interestingly, the mitochondrial membrane potential of Lrrk2 KO BMDMs was normalized after treatment with Mdivi-1 to inhibit DRP1 (Figure 5E–F), suggesting that misregulation of DRP1 occurs upstream of LRRK2-dependent defects in mitochondrial membrane potential.
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claims.claim: Treatment with mitoTEMPO dramatically rescues basal ISG expression in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
claims.source: To test whether ROS could contribute to the defective type I IFN signature in Lrrk2 KO cells, we treated Lrrk2 HET and KO BMDMs with mitoTEMPO (mitoT), a mitochondrially-targeted scavenger of superoxide (Liang et al., 2010). Consistent with oxidative stress driving misregulation of the type I IFN response in the absence of LRRK2, we observed a dramatic rescue of basal ISG expression in Lrrk2 KO cells treated with mitoT (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Addition of sodium pyruvate to growth media increases basal levels of type I IFN in macrophages and MEFs lacking LRRK2.
claims.source: Remarkably, addition of as little as 1 mM sodium pyruvate to the growth media increased the already high basal levels of type I IFN in macrophages and MEFs lacking LRRK2 (Figure 6A–B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that increasing metabolic demands on mitochondria promotes further leakage of mtDNA into the cytosol in these cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claims.claim: Mitochondria in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs are defective in both maximal and reserve respiratory capacity.
claims.source: We found that mitochondria in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs were defective in both maximal and reserve respiratory capacity (Figure 6C, top panels), indicating reduced OXPHOS.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Seahorse metabolic analyzer data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Lrrk2 KO macrophages have reduced glycolysis.
claims.source: Lrrk2 KO macrophages were also defective in non-glycolytic acidification and had reduced glycolysis. (Figure 6C, bottom panels).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Seahorse metabolic analyzer data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Co-treatment of Lrrk2 KO BMDMs with mitoT and IFN-β neutralizing antibody completely restores OXPHOS and glycolysis.
claims.source: Remarkably, co-treatment of Lrrk2 KO BMDMs with mitoT and IFN-β neutralizing antibody completely restored OXPHOS and glycolysis. This rescue was greater than treatment of either IFN-β blockade or mitoT alone (Figure 6C–D), indicating that mitochondrial ROS and constitutive IFNAR signaling independently contribute to the metabolic defects in Lrrk2 KO macrophages.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Seahorse metabolic analyzer data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claims.claim: Lrrk2 KO BMDMs have lower levels of inosine monophosphate (IMP) and hypoxanthine.
claims.source: In Lrrk2 KO BMDMs, we found lower levels of inosine monophosphate (IMP) and hypoxanthine, two intermediates in the purine biosynthesis pathway, which we validated using pure molecular weight standards (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC/MS/MS data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Lrrk2 KO MEFs have significantly fewer de novo biosynthesis puncta containing FGAMS per cell compared to HET controls.
claims.source: Moreover, in accordance with lower levels of purine metabolites, we observed significantly fewer de novo biosynthesis puncta containing formylglycinamidine ribonucleotide synthase (FGAMS, also known as PFAS), a core purinosome component, per Lrrk2 KO MEF cell compared to HET controls (Figure 7C–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7C-D.

claims.claim: Addition of urate reduces basal ISG expression in a dose-dependent fashion in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs and Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 cells.
claims.source: To test this, we first supplemented cells with antioxidants in order to rescue the type I IFN defect in Lrrk2 KO macrophages. Addition of urate, a free radical scavenger and major breakdown product of purine metabolism (Figure 7B), reduced basal ISG expression in a dose-dependent fashion in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs and in Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 cells (Figure 7E–F, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7E-F.

claims.claim: Treatment with urate or mitoT restores the resting mitochondrial membrane potential of Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
claims.source: Furthermore, treatment with urate or mitoT restored the resting mitochondrial membrane potential of Lrrk2 KO BMDMs (Figure 7G–H), suggesting that radical oxygen species contribute to mitochondrial depolarization in the absence of LRRK2.
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7G-H.

claims.claim: Neither urate nor mitoT is sufficient to alter DRP1 activation in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
claims.source: Neither urate nor mitoT was sufficient to alter DRP1 activation in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs, suggesting the antioxidant defects are either downstream or independent of LRRK2-dependent DRP1 misregulation (Figure 7I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7I.

claims.claim: There is a significant increase in CFUs recovered from Lrrk2 KO BMDMs at 5 days following Mtb infection.
claims.source: Lrrk2 HET and KO BMDMs were infected with Mtb (Erdman strain; MOI = 1), and colony forming units (CFUs) were measured over the course of five days. We observed a significant increase in CFUs recovered at 5 days (120 hr) following infection (Figure 8A), suggesting that while Lrrk2 KO macrophages can control Mtb replication early after infection, they are more permissive once the bacteria have established a niche.
claims.evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: There is no difference in survival time of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO mice compared to HET controls.
claims.source: We observed no difference in the survival time of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO mice compared to HET controls (Figure 8B), and at Days 7, 21, 63, and 126 days post-infection, we observed no significant differences in bacterial burdens in the lungs or spleens of infected mice (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: There are no significant differences in bacterial burdens in the lungs or spleens of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO and HET mice at Days 7, 21, 63, and 126 post-infection.
claims.source: We observed no difference in the survival time of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO mice compared to HET controls (Figure 8B), and at Days 7, 21, 63, and 126 days post-infection, we observed no significant differences in bacterial burdens in the lungs or spleens of infected mice (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Major NF-κB pathway inflammatory cytokines (Tnfa, Il6, Il1b) are expressed at similar levels in the lungs of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO and HET mice at Day 21.
claims.source: While major NF-κB pathway inflammatory cytokines (e.g. Tnfa, Il6, Il1b) were expressed at similar levels in the lungs of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO and HET mice at Day 21 (Figure 8E), we observed lower levels of several canonical ISGs including Mx1, Irf9, and Gbp8 (Figure 8F), consistent with trends we observed in Lrrk2 KO macrophages ex vivo (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data from lung homogenates shown in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: Lower levels of ISGs including Mx1, Irf9, and Gbp8 are observed in the lungs of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO mice at Day 21.
claims.source: While major NF-κB pathway inflammatory cytokines (e.g. Tnfa, Il6, Il1b) were expressed at similar levels in the lungs of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO and HET mice at Day 21 (Figure 8E), we observed lower levels of several canonical ISGs including Mx1, Irf9, and Gbp8 (Figure 8F), consistent with trends we observed in Lrrk2 KO macrophages ex vivo (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data from lung homogenates shown in Figure 8F.

claims.claim: Significantly more inflammatory granulomatous nodules are observed in the lungs of Lrrk2 KO mice at Day 21 post-Mtb infection, specifically in the perivascular region.
claims.source: We observed significantly more inflammatory granulomatous nodules in the lungs, specifically in the perivascular region (Figure 8G–H), indicating that more macrophages had infiltrated infected lungs of Lrrk2 KO mice at Day 21 post-infection.
claims.evidence: This is supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 8G-H.

claims.claim: More total neutrophils and more degenerate neutrophils are observed in the lungs of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO mice compared to controls.
claims.source: Consistent with increased inflammation, we observed more total neutrophils (polymorphonuclear leukocytes, PMNs) as well as more PMNs undergoing cell death (degenerate PMNs) in the lungs of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO mice compared to controls (Figure 8I–J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 8I-J.

claims.claim: 4 hr is a key innate immune time point during Mtb infection, corresponding to the peak of transcriptional activation downstream of several pattern recognition receptors.
claims.source: Previous studies have identified 4 hr as a key innate immune time point during Mtb infection, corresponding to the peak of transcriptional activation downstream of several pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), including the cytosolic DNA sensor cGAS (Manzanillo et al., 2012; Watson et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Mycobacterium leprae shares a virulence-associated ESX-1 secretion system with Mtb.
claims.source: We began by infecting macrophages with Mycobacterium leprae (Mlep), which shares a virulence-associated ESX-1 secretion system with Mtb and also induces type I IFN through cytosolic nucleic acid sensing (de Toledo-Pinto et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about M. leprae, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Mycobacterium leprae induces type I IFN through cytosolic nucleic acid sensing.
claims.source: We began by infecting macrophages with Mycobacterium leprae (Mlep), which shares a virulence-associated ESX-1 secretion system with Mtb and also induces type I IFN through cytosolic nucleic acid sensing (de Toledo-Pinto et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: ISD is recognized by cGAS and stimulates the STING/TBK1/IRF3 axis.
claims.source: Transfection of immunostimulatory dsDNA (ISD), which is recognized by cGAS and stimulates the STING/TBK1/IRF3 axis, induced blunted Ifnb expression in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs (Figure 2B), Lrrk2 KO peritoneal macrophages (PEM) (significant differences in Ifnb expression were measured between Lrrk2 KO and HET at baseline but induction differences failed to reach statistical significance via 2-way ANOVA Tukey post-hoc testing) (Figure 2C), Lrrk2 KO RAW 264.7 macrophages (Figure 2D), Lrrk2 KO mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) (Figure 2E), and Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 macrophages (Figure 2F).

claims.source: With lowered resting type I IFN levels, cGas/Lrrk2 double KOs were able to respond normally to IFN/ISG-generating innate immune stimuli like DMXAA, which bypasses cGAS and stimulates STING directly (Diner et al., 2013), and poly(I:C) transfection (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Mtb is a potent activator of type I IFN expression through perturbation of the Mtb-containing phagosome and release of bacterial dsDNA into the cytosol.
claims.source: Mtb is a potent activator of type I IFN expression, thought to occur mostly through perturbation of the Mtb-containing phagosome and release of bacterial dsDNA into the cytosol, where it is detected by DNA sensors like cGAS, activating the STING/TBK1/IRF3 axis (Collins et al., 2015; Wassermann et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2015; Wiens and Ernst, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is a potent activator of type I IFNs downstream of cGAS.
claims.source: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) has been shown to be a potent activator of type I IFNs downstream of cGAS (West et al., 2015), and LRRK2 is known to influence mitochondrial homeostasis (Singh et al., 2019), albeit through mechanisms that are not entirely clear.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Tfam HET mice have high levels of cytosolic mtDNA.

Tfam HET mice are deficient in the mitochondrial transcription factor required for maintaining the mtDNA network and thus have high levels of cytosolic mtDNA (Kasashima et al., 2011; West et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.source: We next sought to rescue type I IFN defects in Lrrk2 KO macrophages by depleting mtDNA using ddC (2',3'-dideoxycytidine), an inhibitor of mtDNA synthesis (Leibowitz, 1971; Meyer and Simpson, 1969).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: LRRK2 contributes to mitochondrial homeostasis through interaction with the mitochondrial fission protein DRP1 in microglia.
claims.source: Previous studies of microglia have shown that LRRK2 contributes to mitochondrial homeostasis through interaction with the mitochondrial fission protein DRP1 (Ho et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: DRP1 is positively regulated via phosphorylation at Ser616.
claims.source: Because DRP1 is known to be positively regulated via phosphorylation at Ser616 (Taguchi et al., 2007), we performed flow cytometry with an antibody specific for phospho-S616 DRP1 and observed significantly higher levels of phospho-S616 DRP1 in Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 cells, Lrrk2 KO BMDMs, and Lrrk2 KO MEFs compared to controls (Figure 4A,C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Macrophages typically switch from OXPHOS to glycolysis when activated.
claims.source: This result was surprising as macrophages typically switch from OXPHOS to glycolysis when activated (Kelly and O'Neill, 2015), but Lrrk2 KO macrophages have reduced utilization of both energy producing pathways.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in immunometabolism, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Purine metabolism is tightly associated with generation of antioxidant compounds.
claims.source: Interestingly, purine metabolism is tightly associated with generation of antioxidant compounds, and several metabolites in this pathway are well-characterized biomarkers of Parkinson's disease (Figure 7B; Zhou et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Several metabolites in the purine metabolism pathway are well-characterized biomarkers of Parkinson's disease.
claims.source: Interestingly, purine metabolism is tightly associated with generation of antioxidant compounds, and several metabolites in this pathway are well-characterized biomarkers of Parkinson's disease (Figure 7B; Zhou et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Urate is a free radical scavenger and major breakdown product of purine metabolism.
claims.source: Addition of urate, a free radical scavenger and major breakdown product of purine metabolism (Figure 7B), reduced basal ISG expression in a dose-dependent fashion in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs and in Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 cells (Figure 7E–F, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about urate's biochemical properties.

claims.claim: LRRK2 missense mutations are associated with exacerbated inflammation and poor disease outcomes in leprosy patients.
claims.source: These data help explain why LRRK2 missense mutations are associated with exacerbated inflammation and poor disease outcomes in leprosy patients (Fava et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Type I IFNs are important biomarkers of Mtb infection associated with poor outcomes in humans and in mouse models of infection.
claims.source: Mtb is a potent activator of cytosolic DNA sensing (Manzanillo et al., 2012; Watson et al., 2012), and type I IFNs are important biomarkers of Mtb infection associated with poor outcomes in humans and in mouse models of infection (Berry et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: IFNAR signaling is required for nitric oxide production in macrophages ex vivo.
claims.source: New insights into the requirement of IFNAR signaling for nitric oxide production in macrophages ex vivo suggest critical roles for type I IFN induction in cell-intrinsic control of Mtb replication (Banks et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claims.claim: Loss of cGAS almost completely abrogates type I IFN expression in macrophages.
claims.source: Our previous experiments demonstrated that while loss of cGAS almost completely abrogates type I IFN expression in macrophages, it has only minor effects in vivo (serum IFN-β levels and lung type I IFN/ISG expression levels) (Collins et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2015), suggesting that Mtb infection can elicit type I IFN expression in important cGAS-independent ways in vivo that we do not yet fully understand.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claims.claim: Loss of cGAS has only minor effects on type I IFN expression in vivo during Mtb infection.
claims.source: Our previous experiments demonstrated that while loss of cGAS almost completely abrogates type I IFN expression in macrophages, it has only minor effects in vivo (serum IFN-β levels and lung type I IFN/ISG expression levels) (Collins et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2015), suggesting that Mtb infection can elicit type I IFN expression in important cGAS-independent ways in vivo that we do not yet fully understand.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claims.claim: A recent publication reported a significant decrease in CFUs in Lrrk2 KO mice at very early infection time points (Day 7 and 14) during Mtb infection.
claims.source: Another recent publication that investigated the role of LRRK2 in controlling Mtb infection does report a significant decrease in CFUs in Lrrk2 KO mice at very early infection time points (Day 7 and 14), which correlates with increased inflammation in the lungs (as we also report) (Härtlova et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claims.claim: LRRK2 inhibitors are a major area of drug development for the treatment of PD.
claims.source: Because LRRK2 inhibitors are a major area of drug development for the treatment of PD, it is crucial to understand how both loss of and mutations in this protein might impact the ability of patients receiving such therapies to respond to and clear infection.

claims.claim: Mtb infection can elicit type I IFN expression in important cGAS-independent ways in vivo.
claims.source: Our previous experiments demonstrated that while loss of cGAS almost completely abrogates type I IFN expression in macrophages, it has only minor effects in vivo (serum IFN-β levels and lung type I IFN/ISG expression levels) (Collins et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2015), suggesting that Mtb infection can elicit type I IFN expression in important cGAS-independent ways in vivo that we do not yet fully understand.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from previous experimental data cited.

results.result: Loss of LRRK2 in macrophages results in elevated basal expression of type I interferon and interferon-stimulated genes. RNA-seq analysis revealed hundreds of genes with significantly higher expression in uninfected Lrrk2 KO macrophages compared to HET controls, with well-characterized ISGs (Mx1, Ifit1, Irf7, Rsad2) expressed several times higher. Pathway analysis identified 'Interferon signaling' and 'Activation of IRF by cytosolic PRRs' as the top enriched pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C36, C37, and C38 are strongly supported by converging evidence from RNA-seq (Figure 1A), RT-qPCR validation (Figure 1E), and unbiased pathway analysis (Figure 1B). The data consistently demonstrate elevated basal ISG expression across multiple experimental approaches and cell types.

results.result: Lrrk2 KO macrophages exhibit blunted interferon responses to mycobacterial pathogens and cytosolic nucleic acid agonists. Despite elevated baseline ISG expression, Lrrk2 KO macrophages fail to induce ISGs to the same levels as controls following Mtb infection, M. leprae infection, or stimulation with ISD and DMXAA. This blunted response is specific to type I IFN pathways, as NF-κB gene expression (Tnfa) remains intact.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C39, C40, C43, C44, and C45 are well-supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 1C), RT-qPCR validation across multiple cell types (Figures 1E-F, 2A-G), and western blot analysis showing reduced phospho-STAT1 (Figure 2H). The specificity of the defect is demonstrated by intact Tnfa responses.

results.result: Lrrk2 KO macrophages show defects in IFNAR signaling and cytosolic DNA sensing. Western blot analysis revealed a significant defect in phospho-STAT1 activation and a modest defect in phospho-IRF3 activation following ISD transfection. Lrrk2 KO BMDMs are also defective in ISG expression following direct IFN-β treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C46, C47, and C48 are supported by western blot data (Figure 2H) and RT-qPCR analysis (Figure 2J). The quantification shows clear reductions in both phospho-STAT1 and phospho-IRF3, with the STAT1 defect being more pronounced, consistent with the observed ISG induction defects.

results.result: Elevated basal type I IFN in Lrrk2 KO macrophages is dependent on chronic IFNAR signaling and can be rescued by blocking this pathway. Treatment with IFN-β neutralizing antibody or genetic deletion of IFNAR reduces basal ISG levels in Lrrk2 KO cells. Loss of cGAS similarly reduces basal ISG expression and restores normal responses to DMXAA and poly(I:C), with restoration of STAT1 phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C49, C50, C51, C52, and C53 are strongly supported by RT-qPCR data from antibody blocking experiments (Figure 2K), genetic crosses with Ifnar KO mice (Figure 2L), and cGas/Lrrk2 double KO experiments (Figures 3A-B). The rescue of both baseline and induction phenotypes provides compelling evidence for the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Mitochondrial defects in Lrrk2 KO macrophages promote mtDNA leakage into the cytosol and chronic cGAS engagement. Lrrk2 KO cells exhibit fragmented mitochondrial networks and ~3-fold higher cytosolic mtDNA levels. Exacerbating mitochondrial defects by depleting TFAM increases basal ISG expression, while depleting mtDNA with ddC normalizes both basal ISG levels and restores IFN-β induction capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C31, C32, C54, C55, C56, C57, C58, and C59 are well-supported by immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 3C), qPCR measurements of cytosolic mtDNA (Figure 3E), western blot controls (Figure 3F), and genetic and pharmacological rescue experiments (Figures 3G-I). The convergence of gain-of-function (TFAM depletion) and loss-of-function (ddC treatment) approaches strongly supports the causal role of cytosolic mtDNA.

results.result: DRP1-dependent mitochondrial fragmentation contributes to altered innate immune gene expression in Lrrk2 KO macrophages. Lrrk2 KO cells show significantly higher levels of phospho-S616 DRP1. Chemical inhibition of DRP1 with Mdivi-1 returns ISG expression to control levels, restores cytosolic mtDNA to normal, and normalizes mitochondrial membrane potential.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C60, C61, C62, and C65 are supported by flow cytometry data showing elevated phospho-S616 DRP1 (Figures 4A, C, D), western blot confirmation (Figure 4B), and rescue experiments with Mdivi-1 demonstrating normalization of ISG expression (Figure 4E), cytosolic mtDNA (Figure 4F), and membrane potential (Figures 5E-F). The pharmacological rescue provides strong evidence for DRP1's causal role.

results.result: Lrrk2 KO macrophages exhibit mitochondrial membrane potential defects and increased sensitivity to oxidative stress. Flow cytometry analysis using JC-1 and TMRE dyes revealed lower baseline mitochondrial membrane potential in Lrrk2 KO cells and increased sensitivity to rotenone/ATP and FCCP. Treatment with the mitochondrial antioxidant mitoTEMPO dramatically rescues basal ISG expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C63, C64, and C66 are well-supported by flow cytometry data using two independent dyes (JC-1 and TMRE) across multiple cell types (Figures 5A-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), stress challenge experiments (Figures 5C-D), and rescue with mitoTEMPO (Figure 5G). The consistency across methods and cell types strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: Lrrk2 KO macrophages are defective in both oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis, with metabolic defects driven by both mitochondrial ROS and constitutive IFNAR signaling. Addition of sodium pyruvate increases basal type I IFN levels in Lrrk2 KO cells. Seahorse analysis revealed defects in maximal and reserve respiratory capacity as well as reduced glycolysis. Co-treatment with mitoTEMPO and IFN-β neutralizing antibody completely restores both OXPHOS and glycolysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C67, C68, C69, and C70 are supported by RT-qPCR data showing pyruvate effects (Figures 6A-B), Seahorse metabolic analyzer data demonstrating OXPHOS and glycolysis defects (Figure 6C), and rescue experiments showing that both mitoTEMPO and IFN-β blockade are required for complete metabolic restoration (Figures 6C-D). The additive rescue effect provides strong evidence for independent contributions.

results.result: Reduced purine metabolites and antioxidants contribute to mitochondrial damage and type I IFN expression in Lrrk2 KO macrophages. LC/MS/MS analysis revealed lower levels of IMP and hypoxanthine, with fewer purinosome puncta in Lrrk2 KO cells. Addition of urate reduces basal ISG expression in a dose-dependent manner and restores mitochondrial membrane potential, though neither urate nor mitoTEMPO alters DRP1 activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C71, C72, C73, C74, and C75 are supported by LC/MS/MS metabolomics data validated with pure standards (Figure 7A), immunofluorescence microscopy of purinosomes (Figures 7C-D), dose-response experiments with urate (Figures 7E-F), and flow cytometry showing membrane potential rescue (Figures 7G-H). The observation that antioxidants don't affect DRP1 (Figure 7I) appropriately places oxidative stress downstream or independent of DRP1 misregulation.

results.result: Lrrk2 KO mice can control Mtb replication in vivo with no significant differences in bacterial burdens or survival. Ex vivo, Lrrk2 KO BMDMs show increased CFUs at 5 days post-infection. In vivo, no significant differences in CFUs were observed in lungs or spleens at days 7, 21, 63, and 126 post-infection, and survival times were not different between genotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C34, C76, C77, and C78 are supported by CFU data from ex vivo infections (Figure 8A), survival curves (Figure 8B), and longitudinal CFU measurements from infected mice (Figure 8C). The statistical analysis appropriately uses Mann-Whitney tests, and the sample sizes (minimum 5 mice per group) meet the stated power calculations.

results.result: Lrrk2 KO mice exhibit exacerbated inflammation and lower ISG expression in the lungs during Mtb infection. While NF-κB pathway cytokines (Tnfa, Il6, Il1b) are expressed at similar levels, ISGs (Mx1, Irf9, Gbp8) are lower in Lrrk2 KO lungs at day 21. Histopathology reveals significantly more inflammatory granulomatous nodules, particularly in perivascular regions, and increased total and degenerate neutrophils.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C35, C79, C80, C81, and C82 are well-supported by RT-qPCR data from lung homogenates (Figures 8E-F), H&E staining and semi-quantitative scoring (Figures 8G-H), and neutrophil quantification (Figures 8I-J). The consistency between ex vivo and in vivo ISG phenotypes strengthens the conclusions, and the histopathological analysis was performed by a masked, board-certified veterinary pathologist.

results.result: LRRK2's role in maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis is critical for proper induction of type I IFN gene expression in macrophages and for downstream inflammatory responses during in vivo infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C116 and C117 represent the main conclusions of the manuscript and are supported by the totality of experimental evidence linking LRRK2 to mitochondrial homeostasis (DRP1 phosphorylation, membrane potential, mtDNA leakage), type I IFN dysregulation (elevated baseline, blunted induction), and in vivo inflammatory phenotypes. The mechanistic chain from mitochondrial defects through cGAS/IFNAR signaling to immune outcomes is well-established through multiple rescue experiments.

results.result: Expression of non-ISG genes ApoE and Ldhb is reduced in uninfected Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
results.evaluation: Claims C41 and C42 are supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 1G). While these findings are interesting and may have implications for understanding LRRK2's broader cellular roles, they are not central to the main narrative about type I IFN dysregulation and are not mechanistically explored further.

results.result: LRRK2 may play a role in regulating the central nervous system immune milieu in PD patients via alteration of mitochondrial homeostasis in brain-resident glial cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C118 is explicitly speculative and represents an extrapolation from the macrophage findings to potential CNS implications. While the speculation is reasonable given the established role of LRRK2 in PD and the findings in peripheral immune cells, no direct experimental evidence is provided to support this specific claim about CNS immune regulation.

results.result: Proposed mechanisms for the refractory phenotype in Lrrk2 KO macrophages include oxidized cytosolic DNA resistant to TREX-1 or upregulation of unidentified negative regulators.
results.evaluation: Claims C119 and C120 are explicitly speculative proposals to explain the unusual refractory phenotype where high basal IFN leads to blunted responses rather than enhanced responses. While the oxidized DNA hypothesis is supported by a citation and is consistent with the data, neither mechanism is directly tested. These remain plausible but unvalidated hypotheses.

results.result: Loss of LRRK2 could alter DRP1 phosphorylation indirectly through changing serine accessibility, protein-protein interactions, or by modifying pathways controlling mitochondrial turnover or lysosome homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C121 and C122 are speculative proposals to explain the observation that Lrrk2 KO cells have elevated phospho-S616 DRP1 despite LRRK2 not being required for this phosphorylation. The proposals are reasonable given that other kinases can phosphorylate DRP1 at this site (C111), but no direct evidence is provided to distinguish between these mechanisms.

results.result: Mtb infection can elicit type I IFN expression in important cGAS-independent ways in vivo that are not yet fully understood.
results.evaluation: Claim C123 is an inference drawn from the authors' previous work (cited as Collins et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2015) showing that cGAS deletion has major effects in macrophages but minor effects in vivo. This inference is appropriately supported by the cited data and helps explain why the in vivo phenotypes in Lrrk2 KO mice are more modest than the ex vivo macrophage phenotypes.
